slides.title: Exponentially weighted averages
slides.body:
filtered version of gradients x(t)

gradients at time t 

filtering parameter Beta
slides.notes:
https://www.coursera.org/lecture/deep-neural-network/exponentially-weighted-averages-duStO  (good video that explains this)


IF Beta = 0.9
current weighted average = 0.9 previous weight average + 0.1 current temp

As a general rule, you could say that the value for a specific day = an average over (1/1-Beta) days’ temperature
So, if it’s 0.1 (beta 0.9) it is as if you are averaging over 10 days, if it’s 0.02 (beta = 0.98), it is as if you are averaging over 50 days), 0.5 => averaging over 2 days (not very smooth)
The more days, the smoother the curve (i.e. the higher beta, the smoother the curve)

Why shifted to right => current temperature affects the curve les (depending on the value of Beta).

slides.title: Gradient Descent with Momentum
slides.body:
Exponentially weighted average of gradients over time 

Momentum:

source

Two hyperparameters
α: Learning rate
β: Controls the exponentially weighted average
slides.notes:
On the vertical axis you want it slower, but on the horizontal axis you want it faster!
Similar to previous formula (temperature)
Now you compute the derivatives (dw, db) on the batch
=> Vdw = Beta(Vdw) + (1-beta)dw

This will smooth out the steps of gradient descent. => on the vertical axis this means it will be close to zero (because it goes up and down… on the x-axis is will average the step on the horizontal axis => more straightforward steps.

The second formula is is the same as the first one, except for the fact that you need to scale your learning rate alfa by a factor (1-beta)

A more intuitive explanation:
=> try and imagine the graph as a being a 3d bowl. and you have a ball that is rolling down the hill of the bowl.  The derivative terms are providing acceleration.
Your beta is the friction (it prevents the ball from speeding up without limit because it’s a number smaller than 1) , Vt-1 - velocity,  your derivatives represent the acceleration. Your ball can now gain momentum and accelerate. 

Now we have two hyperparamters:
Beta and Alfa 
=> Beta usually equal 0.9  => control your exponentially weighted average
=> alfa: learning rate

slides.title: Nesterov Accelerated Momentum
slides.body:
What if we calculate the gradients considering the momentum?
Can that minimize overshooting and oscillation?
slides.notes:
Nesterov momentum is a simple change to normal momentum. Here the gradient term is not computed from the current position θ in parameter space but instead from a position θ+μv. This helps because while the gradient term always points in the right direction (the direction where the loss is minimized), the momentum term may not. If the momentum term points in the wrong direction or overshoots, the gradient can still “go back” and correct it in the same update step.

If we continue the rolling ball analogy:
A ball that rolls down a hill accelerating, blindly following the slope, is highly unsatisfactory. We'd like to have a smarter ball, a ball that has a notion of where it is going so that it knows to slow down before the hill slopes up again.

slides.title: Momentum
slides.body:
Pros	
Faster convergence than traditional SGD. It moves faster because of the momentum it accumulates
Cons
When too much momentum:
Swing back and forth between local minima 
Missing minima
slides.notes: As the ball accelerates down the hill, how do we know that we don't miss the local minima? If the momentum is too much, we will most likely miss the local minima, rolling past it, but then rolling backwards, missing it again. If the momentum is too much, we could just swing back and forward between the local minima.

slides.title: AdaGrad
slides.body: Adaptive Gradient Algorithm

slides.title: AdaGrad
slides.body:
Adagrad uses a different learning rate for each parameter 𝛉i
Smaller rates for parameters associated with frequent features
Larger rate for parameters associated with infrequent features.
slides.notes:
Ιnstead of keeping track of the sum of gradient like momentum, the Adaptive Gradient algorithm, or AdaGrad for short, keeps track of the sum of gradient squared and uses that to adapt the gradient in different directions. 

AdaGrad individually adapts the learning rates of all model parameters by scaling them inversely proportional to the square root of the sum of all the historical squared values of the gradient.

When you have features that occur a lot => you can do small updates,
but for features/word appearing rarely => You need to do bigger updates
Why GloVe embeddings: pretrained embeddings => infrequent words require much larger updates than frequent ones

slides.title: RMSprop
slides.body:
Overcomes the issue of the continuously decreasing learning rate
RMSProp uses a moving average instead of accumulating gradient squares.
slides.notes:
The problem of AdaGrad, however, is that it is incredibly slow. This is because the sum of gradient squared only grows and never shrinks. RMSProp (for Root Mean Square Propagation) fixes this issue by adding a decay factor.

RMSprop
decaying average over past squared gradients E[g2]t in order to discard extreme past history:

The only difference RMSProp has with Adagrad is that the gt term is calculated by exponentially decaying average and not the sum of gradients. More precisely, the sum of gradient squared is actually the decayed sum of gradient squared. The decay rate is saying only recent gradient² matters, and the ones from long ago are basically forgotten. 


RMSprop => Geoff Hinton => Hinton suggests γ to be set to 0.9, while a good default value for the learning rate (η) is 0.001

slides.notes:
Takes the best of both worlds (of Momentum and RMSProp)
=> the go to choice because it empirically works well

In addition to storing an exponentially decaying average of past squared gradients vt like Adadelta and RMSprop, Adam also keeps an exponentially decaying average of past gradients mt, similar to momentum. 
Whereas momentum can be seen as a ball running down a slope, Adam behaves like a heavy ball with friction, which thus prefers flat minima in the error surface [15].
